title: Ports and Scanning
sub: See which programs listen on your Mac, test ports with nc, and map your own LAN with nmap, ethically
goals: Explain sockets, ports and the five-part tuple that identifies a connection
Read TCP states in netstat output and say what CLOSE_WAIT or TIME_WAIT piles mean
Find which process owns a port with lsof, and free the port safely
Test, listen on and transfer data over a port with nc
Run host-discovery and port scans with nmap on networks you own, and parse the results with awk
Build lan-inventory, a script that turns your LAN into a CSV of hosts and services

blocks.text: An IP address gets a packet to the right machine; a **port** gets it to the right program on that machine. Every service you run, every server you reach and every tool in this book that talks over a network is a story about ports. In this chapter you will list what is listening on your Mac, open and close ports yourself with `nc`, learn the TCP states that `netstat` prints, and then use `nmap` to survey your own network the way an administrator or an attacker would, which is the best way to understand what your devices expose. The chapter ends with `lan-inventory`, a script that finds every device on your LAN and records its open services.

Port scanning is routine for administrators and also the first step of an attack, so the line is **authorization**. In this chapter you may scan: your own Mac (`127.0.0.1`), machines on your own home network that you own or administer (`{{labhost}}`, your router, your NAS, your Pi), and `scanme.nmap.org`, which the Nmap project explicitly permits for light use. Do not scan your school, your employer, a hotel or café network, your neighbors, or any address you are unsure about. A full section on rules, laws and log footprints comes before the first `nmap` command.
Sockets and ports

A **socket** is the endpoint a program uses to send and receive over the network. When a program asks the kernel for a socket, it chooses a protocol (TCP or UDP) and the kernel hands back a file descriptor, one more thing that is "a file" in Unix. A **port** is a 16-bit number (0 to 65535) that the kernel uses to route arriving data to the right socket.

A server **binds** a socket to a port and **listens**. A client connects from a temporary port the kernel picks. A TCP connection is identified by five values, the **5-tuple**, and the kernel keeps one table entry per tuple:

blocks.code:
protocol   local IP        local port   remote IP        remote port
   ────────   ─────────────   ──────────   ──────────────   ───────────
   TCP        192.168.1.23    ⟪y:52814⟫        140.82.121.3     ⟪c:443⟫      your browser to a web server
   TCP        192.168.1.23    ⟪y:52815⟫        140.82.121.3     ⟪c:443⟫      second tab: same server, new local port
   TCP        192.168.1.50    ⟪c:22⟫           192.168.1.23     ⟪y:51002⟫    the Pi's sshd serving you

   One server port (22, 443) serves thousands of clients, because each client
   arrives with a different (remote IP, remote port) pair.

IANA divides the 65536 ports into three ranges:

head: Range
Name
Use
rows: standard services: 22 ssh, 53 dns, 80 http, 443 https
applications by convention: 3306 MySQL, 5432 Postgres, 8080 alternate http
chosen by the kernel for the client side of connections

blocks.text: macOS uses 49152 to 65535 for ephemeral ports (check with `sysctl net.inet.ip.portrange.first net.inet.ip.portrange.last`), which is why the browser connections you see in `netstat` all have local ports like `52814`. Each outgoing connection uses one, and this range is what limits how many simultaneous connections one client can open to the same server.
Where a server listens
The **bind address** decides who can reach a server. It is the most important setting in any server's configuration and the reason `--bind 127.0.0.1` appeared in the last chapter.

head: Bind address
Shown by netstat/lsof as
Who can connect
rows: machines that can reach that interface
anyone who can reach any of this Mac's addresses

blocks.text: Traditional Unix requires root to bind a port under 1024. Since macOS 10.14 (Mojave) a normal user can bind them on all interfaces, so `python3 -m http.server 80` works without `sudo`. If you still meet "Permission denied" on a low port, use one above 1024.
TCP states, as netstat shows them

TCP is a connection with a lifecycle, and the kernel records which stage each connection is in. You met the three-way handshake in [Network basics](#networks); here it is as states, because `netstat` prints exactly these words.

blocks.code:
CLIENT                                          SERVER
                                                    LISTEN   (waiting on port 80)
   SYN_SENT     ── SYN ────────────────────────▶    SYN_RCVD
   ESTABLISHED  ◀─ SYN+ACK ─────────────────────
                ── ACK ────────────────────────▶    ESTABLISHED
                      ... data flows both ways ...
   FIN_WAIT_1   ── FIN ────────────────────────▶    CLOSE_WAIT   (app has not closed yet)
   FIN_WAIT_2   ◀─ ACK ─────────────────────────
                                                     app calls close()
   TIME_WAIT    ◀─ FIN ─────────────────────────    LAST_ACK
                ── ACK ────────────────────────▶    CLOSED
   (waits a while, then CLOSED)

head: State
Meaning
What it tells you when you see it
rows: a server socket waiting for connections
the service is up on that port
this side sent a SYN and waits
stuck here means the remote end is not answering (firewall, host down)
many of these can mean a SYN flood or a slow client
this side closed first and awaits the peer
brief; long stays mean the peer is not closing
the peer closed, this side's program has not
**an application bug**: it forgot to call close() on a socket
this side sent its own FIN after the peer's
connection closed, kernel keeps the entry a little longer

blocks.text: **TIME_WAIT** exists so that stray delayed packets from the old connection cannot be mistaken for a new one that reuses the same 5-tuple. The side that closes first holds the entry for a short multiple of the maximum segment lifetime, which macOS exposes as `sysctl net.inet.tcp.msl` (15000 ms by default). Thousands of TIME_WAIT lines after a burst of short requests are normal. Thousands of **CLOSE_WAIT** lines are not: the kernel is waiting for your program to finish closing, and the number grows until it runs out of file descriptors.

blocks.title: Why a closed port answers differently from a silent one

blocks.text: A host with nothing listening on a port replies to a SYN with a RST ("connection refused") immediately. A host behind a firewall that drops the packet sends nothing, and the client waits for a timeout. Those two behaviors, a fast refusal versus silence, are exactly what scanners use to tell **closed** from **filtered** ports, and what you see as the difference between `Connection refused` and `Operation timed out` in `nc`.
UDP in one section

**UDP** has no connection, no handshake and no states. A program sends a datagram to an address and port and hopes. If nothing listens, the kernel typically answers with an ICMP "port unreachable", and that is the only feedback. Because UDP is fast and light, it carries DNS (53), DHCP (67/68), NTP time (123), mDNS/Bonjour (5353), many games, VoIP and QUIC (443, used by HTTP/3). In `netstat -an` a UDP socket has no state column; in `lsof` it appears as `UDP *:5353`.

The consequence for diagnosis: you cannot "connect" to a UDP port to test it. A silent port is either open (it accepted the datagram and said nothing) or filtered, and the tools can only report `open|filtered`. UDP scans are therefore slow and ambiguous, and you will use them rarely.
Well-known ports
You will recognize the following from every network you work on. The table below is searchable; each row includes a ready-made `nc -zv` test.
Who is listening on this Mac
Start with the machine in front of you. Two commands answer "what is open and who owns it": `netstat` shows the kernel's socket table, and `lsof` ties each socket to a process.

blocks.name: netstat
blocks.sum: Print the kernel's network tables: active sockets and their TCP state, interface counters and protocol statistics.

how.text: With `-a` and `-n`, `netstat` lists every socket the kernel knows: listening servers and established connections, with local address, foreign address and TCP state. `-n` prints numbers instead of resolving names, which is faster and exact. Addresses print as `address.port`, with a **dot** before the port (`192.168.1.23.52814`), and `*` means "any address".

macOS `netstat` is the BSD one. There is no `-p PID` or `-t`/`-l`/`-u` as on Linux, and no `ss`; `-p` selects a *protocol* (`tcp`, `udp`). The columns do not include the process. To map a socket to a program use `lsof`, or add `-v`, which on current macOS adds extra columns including the owning PID.
The same tool shows routes (`-r`), interface counters (`-i`, with `-b` for bytes) and per-protocol statistics (`-s`), which count retransmissions, resets and refused connections.

flags.d: Include server (listening) sockets, not only connections.
Numeric addresses and ports; no DNS or service-name lookups.
Limit to one protocol: `tcp`, `udp` and a few others.
More columns; on recent macOS this includes process IDs.
Per-protocol statistics (add `-p tcp` to narrow).
Interface table with packet and error counts; `-b` adds byte counts.
Routing table (see [Addressing](#addressing)).
Do not truncate long addresses.

gotchas: IPv4 and IPv6 are separate lines (`tcp4`, `tcp6`). A server listening on `*` can appear twice, once per family, and a count of "listeners" may be doubled.
`$NF` is the last field, which is the state for TCP rows, but UDP rows have no state, so filter by protocol first.
Ports in `address.port` are separated from the IP by the last dot. For IPv4 strip them with `sed 's/\.[0-9]*$//'`. IPv6 addresses have no such clean shape.

blocks.name: lsof -i
blocks.sum: List the network sockets that processes hold open, with the process name, PID and user: the answer to "who is using this port".

how.text: [System management](#system) introduced `lsof` as "list open files". Here the filter `-i` selects only network files. The argument is a pattern: `-i :8000` (any protocol, port 8000), `-i TCP:80`, `-i @192.168.1.50` (connections to or from that host), `-i 4` (IPv4 only). `-n` skips DNS lookups and `-P` skips service-name lookups, so you see `8000` and not `irdmi`; use `-nP` always.

`-sTCP:LISTEN` restricts to listening sockets, or `-sTCP:ESTABLISHED` to live connections. Selectors normally combine with OR; `-a` makes them AND, so `lsof -a -p 1234 -i` means "network files of PID 1234". Without `sudo` you see only your own processes; add `sudo` to see every user's.

gotchas: As a normal user `lsof` shows only your processes, so a port can look free while a root daemon holds it. If `lsof -i :PORT` is empty but binding fails, try `sudo`.
`kill $(lsof -t ...)` with an empty match runs `kill` with no argument and prints a usage error. Look at the output first.
A closed listener can leave the port busy for a while in `TIME_WAIT`. Servers that set `SO_REUSEADDR` can rebind at once; many scripts do not, and report `Address already in use`.

blocks.text: Notice that the same fact appears three ways: `lsof` names the process (`Python`, PID 51234), `netstat` shows the state (`LISTEN`), and after your `curl` the server side of the finished connection lingers briefly in `TIME_WAIT` with the client's ephemeral port, `52950`. Stop the server with Control-C and run `lsof` again: the row is gone.
In a third tab run `lsof -nP -r 1 -i :8000`, which repeats once a second. Start and stop the server, and hit it with `curl`, and watch the rows appear and disappear.
Many programs you did not start are listening too. List them and decide which you recognize:

blocks.code:
$ sudo lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN | awk 'NR > 1 {print $1, $2, $9}' | sort -u | column -t
ControlCe  612    *:5000
ControlCe  612    *:7000
rapportd   498    *:49152
Python     51234  127.0.0.1:8000

blocks.text: On recent macOS, `ControlCe` (Control Center) listens on 5000 and 7000 for **AirPlay Receiver**. That is why a Flask app that defaults to port 5000 fails with `Address already in use` on a Mac: turn AirPlay Receiver off in System Settings, or use another port. `rapportd` supports Continuity features such as Handoff.

blocks.name: nettop
blocks.sum: A live, top-style view of network use per process or per connection.

how.text: `nettop` reads the same socket and interface statistics as `netstat` and shows, for each process and its sockets, bytes in and out, updated every second. It answers "which program is using the network right now", which `lsof` and `netstat` cannot. It is interactive: press `q` to quit, and the on-screen help lists the keys for sorting and expanding.

flags.d: Show only TCP sockets (`udp` or `route` also work). The default is TCP and UDP.
Do not resolve addresses to names.

Logging mode: write N samples as CSV to stdout and exit, instead of the interactive view.

gotchas: The CSV column layout varies between macOS releases. Print the header row with `head -3` and pick columns by name before you script around it.

blocks.text: Talking to a port with nc

`nc` (netcat) is the TCP/UDP Swiss army knife: it connects a socket to your standard input and output. That makes it a port tester, a banner grabber, a one-line server, a file mover and, because everything is text, a way to speak a protocol by hand. The macOS `nc` is a BSD netcat; its flags differ from the GNU or Nmap versions, and `man nc` on your Mac is the authority.

blocks.name: nc
blocks.sum: Open a TCP or UDP connection, or listen for one, and connect it to stdin and stdout.
blocks.syntax: nc [-vzu] [-w secs] host port|range      nc -l [-k] [-u] port

how.text: As a **client**, `nc host port` opens a TCP connection and then copies stdin to the socket and the socket to stdout, so what you type is sent and what arrives is printed. As a **server**, `nc -l port` binds the port, waits for one connection, then does the same copying. Pipes and redirects make it a data mover: `nc -l 9000 > file` receives, `nc host 9000 < file` sends.

`-z` ("zero I/O") connects and immediately closes, which is a port test: exit status 0 means the connection was accepted. Add `-v` for a sentence about the result and `-w 2` to give up after 2 seconds, so a filtered port does not hang you. `-u` switches to UDP.
On macOS the listener takes the port as an argument (`nc -l 9000`); do not add `-p` with `-l`. A listener serves one connection and exits unless you add `-k` to keep listening.

flags.d: Scan: connect and close without sending data.
Verbose: report success and failure.
Time out the connection attempt (and idle connections) after SECS.
Listen for an incoming connection instead of connecting.
Keep listening for another connection after the current one ends (with `-l`).
Use UDP.
Numeric only; no DNS.
Force IPv4 or IPv6.

gotchas: A **refused** connection (`Connection refused`) is instant and means the host is up but nothing listens. A **timeout** (`Operation timed out`) means the packets are being dropped, usually by a firewall, or the host is off.
`nc -zu` for UDP reports "succeeded" when no ICMP port-unreachable comes back, which includes ports that are filtered. Treat a UDP "open" from `nc` as a hint, not proof.
After a file transfer the sender may sit open waiting for the other side. `-w 3` ends it after 3 idle seconds; Control-C works too.
notes: On recent macOS `nc -v` prints extra lines about the connection (interface, source and destination ports) before the "succeeded" sentence, and failures read `nc: connectx to HOST port N (tcp) failed: ...`. Older releases say `connect to`. Pipe through `grep succeeded` to keep it simple.

blocks.text: A chat in two tabs
Open two Terminal tabs. In tab one, listen on a port above 1024 on loopback only:
In tab two, connect and type a line:

blocks.code:
$ nc 127.0.0.1 9000
hello from tab two

blocks.text: The line appears in tab one; type a reply there and it appears in tab two. Press Control-C in either tab to end it. You have just built a TCP chat out of two copies of a 30-year-old tool. It is also a diagnostic: if `nc -l` works on a port but remote clients cannot reach it, the problem is the bind address or a firewall, not your program.

blocks.title: nc is a gift to attackers too

blocks.text: Because `nc -l` plus a shell would hand out remote control, never run `nc -l` on a reachable interface and pipe it into `sh` or `zsh`. Bind to `127.0.0.1` for experiments, and remember that anything you leave listening on `0.0.0.0` is reachable by every device on the network.
Scanning: rules first

A **port scan** sends probes to many ports and records how each one answers. Administrators scan to inventory services and find mistakes. Attackers scan to find a way in. The packets are identical, so the only difference is **permission**.

items.text: **Authorization.** Scan only networks you own or have explicit written permission to test. "It was open" and "I was curious" are not permission. Laws such as the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and the UK Computer Misuse Act turn on authorization and intent, and you can still receive a complaint or lose your internet service even when no law is broken.

**Your home network is yours; the one you borrow is not.** Do not scan from work, school, a hotel, a library or café Wi-Fi, a shared flat's network that you do not administer, or a VPN exit that belongs to someone else.

**Test targets.** `scanme.nmap.org` is run by the Nmap project and welcomes light scans, with a request to keep to a few per day and never to run attacks or brute-force tools against it. If it stops resolving, someone abused it.
**Be gentle with fragile devices.** Old printers, IoT cameras and cheap switches sometimes crash under a scan. Start with default timing, a few ports and no scripts, and scan a printer last.

**You leave a footprint.** A scan is visible. A router's log shows a burst of connection attempts from your IP to many ports in sequence, an IDS flags it, and your own firewall may record it. Scanning your own gear is a good way to see what that footprint looks like (see the logs section below).
**Write down why.** A habit from professional work: note the scope (which addresses), the time and the purpose before you scan.

blocks.text: Before every scan, ask: "If the owner of this address asked what I was doing, could I say that I own it or that they asked me to?" If the answer is not an immediate yes, do not send the packets.
nmap: the network mapper

`nmap` is the standard tool for host discovery, port scanning, service identification and basic fingerprinting. It is not part of macOS. Install it with Homebrew (`brew install nmap`), and check with `nmap --version`.
Two questions, two phases
An `nmap` run answers two separate questions, and many options tune one or the other:

items.text: **Host discovery**: which addresses are alive? By default nmap probes first (ping-style packets, and on a local network ARP) and scans only hosts that answer. `-sn` stops after this step, and `-Pn` skips it and scans everything.
**Port scan**: for each live host, what is the state of each port?

blocks.text: Each port is reported in one of these states:

head: State
What nmap saw
Typical meaning
rows: the port answered with a reset (RST)
no answer, or an ICMP error

blocks.text: Connect scan versus SYN scan

The default depends on privilege. As a normal user nmap uses a **connect scan** (`-sT`), which asks the operating system to open each connection completely. With `sudo` it uses a **SYN scan** (`-sS`), which sends a bare SYN and aborts after the reply.

blocks.code:
-sT  connect scan (no root)                -sS  SYN scan (needs sudo)

   you  ── SYN ───────────▶ port             you  ── SYN ───────────▶ port
        ◀─ SYN/ACK ─────── (open)                 ◀─ SYN/ACK ─────── (open)
        ── ACK ───────────▶ handshake done        ── RST ───────────▶ never completes
        ── RST/FIN ────────▶ (service may log it)  (fewer log entries)

   closed port:  ◀─ RST ─────────────         filtered port:  no reply, nmap waits

blocks.text: Both give the same open/closed answer. The connect scan is noisier because services see a full connection, but it needs no privileges. The scan in `scan.txt` is of this kind (`closed tcp ports (conn-refused)`).

blocks.name: nmap
blocks.sum: Discover live hosts, scan their ports and optionally identify services, on networks you are authorized to test.

how.text: `nmap` sends probe packets and classifies the replies. A target can be a name, an address, a range (`192.168.1.10-50`), a CIDR block (`192.168.1.0/24`) or a list from a file (`-iL`). With no port option it scans the 1000 most common ports. Output lists, for each host, the ports that are not closed, each with its state and the service name guessed from the port number.

`-sV` goes further and talks to open ports to read banners and identify the actual software and version; `-O` guesses the operating system from how the TCP stack behaves (needs `sudo`). Scripts from the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) are enabled with `--script`; `-sC` runs the "default" set. More probing means more traffic and more risk to fragile devices, so add features one at a time.
`-T0` to `-T5` are timing templates. `-T4` is a common choice on a fast LAN. Avoid `-T5` and avoid scanning faster than a device can answer.

gotchas: Scanning a whole network with `-sV -A` is slow, loud and risky for fragile devices. Discover first (`-sn`), then scan chosen hosts and ports.
A host that blocks ping looks "down" and is skipped unless you add `-Pn`. On a LAN as root nmap uses ARP, which cannot be blocked, so discovery there is reliable.
`closed` and `filtered` are easy to tell apart on a normal firewall-less home device, but macOS "stealth mode" in its firewall drops probes to closed ports too, turning them into `filtered`.
notes: On macOS 15 and later, the first time a Terminal program touches the local network the system may ask for "Local Network" permission. If scans of LAN hosts fail with "No route to host" or find nothing, check System Settings, Privacy and Security, Local Network.

blocks.text: Reading a scan
The lab file `scan.txt` is a saved scan of five devices. Read one block line by line:

blocks.code:
Nmap scan report for pi.lan (192.168.1.50)
Host is up (0.0043s latency).
Not shown: 997 closed tcp ports (conn-refused)
PORT     STATE SERVICE
22/tcp   open  ssh
80/tcp   open  http
8080/tcp open  http-proxy

blocks.text: `pi.lan (192.168.1.50)` is the name (from reverse DNS) and address. `Host is up (0.0043s latency)` comes from the discovery phase. `Not shown: 997 closed tcp ports (conn-refused)` summarizes the ports nmap did not bother to list, and `conn-refused` is the reason, so this was a connect scan and the closed ports answered with a reset. The table lists everything else: `ssh` (22) means a login service, `http` (80) a web server, and `8080` an alternate web port such as a dashboard. The `SERVICE` name is only the registered name for the port number. `-sV` is what checks what is really there.
Compare it with `scan.txt` using the terminal below. Start by listing the hosts and the number of open ports on each:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk '/^Nmap scan report/ {print $5}' scan.txt
router.lan
pi.lan
nas.lan
printer.lan
homeassistant.lan
$ awk '/^Nmap scan report/ {host=$NF; gsub(/[()]/,"",host)} /^[0-9]+\/tcp +open/ {n[host]++} END {for (h in n) print n[h], h}' scan.txt | sort -rn
4 192.168.1.60
3 192.168.1.50
3 192.168.1.1
2 192.168.1.70
1 192.168.1.90

blocks.text: The first `awk` prints the fifth word of each report line, the name. The second keeps the IP in a variable as it passes each report header (`gsub` strips the parentheses) and counts the `open` lines under it. The NAS at `.60` exposes the most services: ssh, two file-sharing ports (139 and 445) and a web interface on 5000. On a real network that is the host to review first.
A short list of safe NSE scripts

NSE scripts are grouped in categories. The ones that only read and do not attack are `default`, `safe` and `discovery`. Avoid `intrusive`, `brute`, `dos` and `exploit` entirely unless you are doing authorized testing with a plan.

What it reads
Example

blocks.text: Output formats

Humans read the normal output. Programs should read **XML** (`-oX`), which is stable and complete. The **greppable** format (`-oG`) is deprecated but convenient for one-liners, and one host fits on one line:

blocks.code:
Host: 192.168.1.50 (pi.lan)	Status: Up
Host: 192.168.1.50 (pi.lan)	Ports: 22/open/tcp//ssh///, 80/open/tcp//http///, 8080/open/tcp//http-proxy///	Ignored State: closed (997)

blocks.title: Turn greppable nmap output into CSV

tokens.exp: connect scan, no DNS, show only open ports
read targets from a file of your own LAN addresses
greppable output to stdout
split each line on tabs
only lines that have a Ports field
the IP is the second word of the first field
one array element per port entry
port is f[1], state f[2], service f[5]
write ip,port,service

blocks.text: The fields are separated by tabs. In the `Ports:` field each port is `port/state/protocol/owner/service/rpc/version`, so splitting on `/` gives the port number at position 1, the state at 2 and the service at 5. The awk in the card above relies on exactly this.
Other tools for the toolbox

blocks.name: telnet
blocks.sum: A plain-text TCP client, used today to talk to a port by hand and read a banner; not for logins.

how.text: macOS stopped shipping `telnet` years ago; `brew install telnet` brings it back. It opens a TCP connection and lets you type. `nc` does the same job and is installed, so `telnet` is mostly useful when a guide or a device expects it. To leave, press Control-] and type `quit`. Never use it to log in to anything over a network you do not control: Telnet sends passwords in clear text.

examples.desc: Read an SMTP banner on your own mail server

blocks.name: socat
blocks.sum: Connect any two data endpoints, such as a TCP port, a UDP port, a file, a serial device or your terminal.

how.text: `socat` is `nc` with a general endpoint syntax: each side is an address type with comma-separated options (`TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork,reuseaddr`). It copies bytes between the two sides. `fork` makes the listener serve many clients at once and `reuseaddr` lets you restart it immediately. It is the tool for forwarding a port, bridging a serial device to TCP, or testing a client against a fake server.

examples.desc: Forward port 8080 on this Mac to the practice server on 8000
Connect your terminal to a TCP port
Forward, then confirm with the client of your choice

gotchas: A forwarder bound to all interfaces exposes the target to the whole network. Bind to loopback (`TCP-LISTEN:8080,bind=127.0.0.1,fork`) for private tests.

blocks.name: iperf3
blocks.sum: Measure TCP or UDP throughput between two machines, with one running as the server.
blocks.syntax: iperf3 -s      iperf3 -c server [-t secs] [-R] [-u -b rate] [-P n] [-J]

how.text: Unlike a web speed test, `iperf3` measures the path between *your two machines*, so it separates the speed of your Wi-Fi or cable from the speed of the internet. Run `iperf3 -s` on one side (it listens on TCP port 5201) and `iperf3 -c server` on the other. By default the client sends; `-R` reverses the direction so the server sends. `-u` tests UDP and reports jitter and loss.

flags.d: Run as server.
Run as client against HOST.
Test length; the default is 10 seconds.
Reverse: the server sends, the client receives.
UDP at a target bit rate, such as `-b 100M`.
N parallel streams.
JSON output.

examples.desc: Server on the Pi, test from your Mac
Throughput in Mbit/s from the JSON result

gotchas: `Connection refused` usually means the server is not running or a firewall blocks TCP 5201. Wi-Fi tests vary a lot with distance; use `-R` too, since uplink and downlink can differ.

blocks.text: Looking at the Mac's own firewall (read-only)

macOS has two firewalls. The **application firewall** works per app and is what shows the "accept incoming network connections?" dialog; **pf** is the BSD packet filter underneath, normally unused. Reading their state changes nothing:

blocks.code:
/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate
/usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getstealthmode
sudo pfctl -s info | head -3

$ /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getglobalstate
Firewall is disabled. (State = 0)
$ /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --getstealthmode
Stealth mode disabled
$ sudo pfctl -s info | head -3
Status: Disabled

blocks.title: Look, do not change, while learning

blocks.text: The same `socketfilterfw` command has flags that turn the firewall on and off, and `pfctl` can load rules that cut you off from the network. Keep to the `--get...` and `-s ...` forms here. When you are ready to enable the firewall, use System Settings, Network, Firewall, where a mistake is easy to undo.
What a scan looks like from the target

Scan one of your own machines and look at it from the other side, to learn what a scan leaves behind. Start `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1`, then run `nmap -sV -p 8000 127.0.0.1` from another tab and read the server's log: you will see requests that you never made, which are nmap's version-detection probes. A capture shows the same thing at packet level ([Packet capture](#capture)).
What gets noticed by defenders, on any scanner:

items.text: A single source IP touching **many ports in a short time**, often in numeric order (or randomized, which is nmap's default).
**Connections that open and close without sending data** (a connect scan, or a banner grab that never speaks).
A burst of **SYN packets with no follow-up ACK** (a SYN scan).
Probes to ports nothing runs on, a rare thing for normal traffic.

blocks.text: A scan of your own network is also an audit. Every unexpected row is a question: why is the printer listening on 9100 to the whole LAN? Why does the NAS expose a web admin on 5000? Which of these should be reachable only from a laptop, or turned off?
Pipe recipes
The data is `scan.txt` in the lab, so these run in the practice terminal below and on the real nmap output of your own network alike.

blocks.text: Each is a pattern you can reuse:

items.text: **Flatten.** The first `awk` remembers the current host in a variable and prints it on every open-port line. Reports are multi-line, and flattening them to one row per port makes everything after it a simple pipeline.
**Count by key.** `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` ranks ports by how many hosts have them open. Two hosts expose `22` and `80`.
**Find the owner of a fact.** `grep -B8` shows the 8 lines before a match, so it reaches back to the report header. It is a quick-and-dirty join; the flatten step is more reliable.
**Make CSV.** Split the `22/tcp` field on `/` and join with commas, and the result opens in a spreadsheet or loads into Python's `csv`.

blocks.text: Diff two scans
The best use of nmap for a home network is a baseline. Save a scan today, scan again next month, and let `diff` list what changed. Sort first so that order differences do not count:

blocks.code:
sudo nmap -sT -n --open {{subnet}} -oG - | awk -F'\t' '/Ports:/ {split($1, h, " "); sub(/^Ports: /, "", $2); n = split($2, p, ", "); for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {split(p[i], f, "/"); if (f[2] == "open") print h[2] " " f[1]}}' | sort > scan-today.txt
diff scan-last-month.txt scan-today.txt
comm -13 scan-last-month.txt scan-today.txt

blocks.text: `diff` shows every change with `<` for old and `>` for new. `comm -13` prints only lines that appear in the second file alone: the **new** open ports, which are the ones to investigate. Run `comm -23` for ports that disappeared.
Check a port in a loop

blocks.code: while true; do nc -z -w 2 {{labhost}} {{port}} && echo "$(date +%T) up" || echo "$(date +%T) DOWN"; sleep 5; done

blocks.text: That is a crude monitor. When you reboot the Pi, you will see the exact second SSH returns. Stop it with Control-C.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Scanning something you do not own.** The most serious mistake. See the rules above.
**Reading `filtered` as "safe".** A filtered port is hidden, not closed; the service may still run behind the firewall.
**Reading `closed` as "no service".** The service may use another port, or listen only on loopback.
**Trusting `SERVICE` names.** nmap names a port from its number. Port 80 can run anything; `-sV` checks.
**`netstat -p PID` and `ss`.** Those are Linux. On macOS use `lsof -i` and `netstat -an -p tcp`.
**Binding to `0.0.0.0` by accident.** Test servers bound to all interfaces are visible to the LAN. Bind to `127.0.0.1` unless you want sharing.
**Forgetting `-n`.** Without it nmap and `lsof` do reverse DNS lookups on each address and pause on every one.
**`nc -l -p PORT` on macOS.** The `-p` is for the source port on a client; `-l` takes the port as a plain argument.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Who owns port 8000?

task.text: Start `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` in one tab. In another tab, print the PID and command name of whatever is listening on port 8000, using `lsof`. Then stop the server by PID, not by closing the tab, and confirm that the port is free.

hints: `lsof -nP -i :8000` lists the process. `-t` prints only PIDs.
Use the PID with `kill`, then rerun `lsof`; no output means the port is free.

why.text: `lsof` maps the listening socket to the process holding it. `-t` is built for the `kill $(...)` pattern. `kill` sends SIGTERM, which lets the server exit cleanly. A final `lsof` that prints nothing and exits `1` proves the port is free.

blocks.title: Send a file with nc

task.text: With two Terminal tabs on the same Mac, send `~/lab/ips.txt` through port 9100 to a file called `ips-copy.txt`, using only `nc`. Then verify that the two files are identical.

hints: One tab must listen first. The receiver redirects stdout into a file.
The sender redirects the file into stdin. Add `-w 2` so the sender exits.
blocks.solution:
# tab 1
nc -l 127.0.0.1 9100 > ips-copy.txt
# tab 2
nc -w 2 127.0.0.1 9100 < ips.txt
# then
diff ips.txt ips-copy.txt && echo identical

why.text: `nc` copies stdin to the socket and the socket to stdout, so redirects turn it into a file transfer. The listener must start first because the sender gets `Connection refused` if nothing is bound to the port.

blocks.title: Parse the saved scan

task.text: Using only `scan.txt` and a pipeline, print the hosts that have port 22 open, one name per line, then print how many open ports each host has, biggest first.

hints: Flatten the scan with awk first, so that each line is `host port`.
For the first part filter the flattened lines with grep for `22/tcp`. For the second, count with an awk array or with `cut | uniq -c`.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab
awk '/^Nmap scan report/ {host=$NF; gsub(/[()]/,"",host)} /^[0-9]+\/tcp +open/ {print host, $1}' scan.txt | grep ' 22/tcp' | cut -d' ' -f1
awk '/^Nmap scan report/ {host=$NF; gsub(/[()]/,"",host)} /^[0-9]+\/tcp +open/ {n[host]++} END {for (h in n) print n[h], h}' scan.txt | sort -rn

why.text: Reports span several lines, so remember the host in a variable and emit it with each port line. After that the problem is the usual filter, count and rank pipeline.

blocks.title: Refused or filtered?

task.text: Test TCP port 9999 on `127.0.0.1` with `nc -zv`. Note the message. Then test the same port on an address that is almost certainly unreachable from your network, such as `192.0.2.1`, with `-w 3`. Explain the difference between the two messages in one sentence.

hints: Use `-w 3` for the second test, or you will wait for a long timeout.

why.text: The first is `Connection refused`: the host answered at once with a reset, so it is up and nothing listens. The second is `Operation timed out`: no answer at all, which is what a silent firewall or an unrouted address looks like. `192.0.2.0/24` is reserved for documentation and is never a real host.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose, then fix it

task.text: Start `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` in one tab and then try to start a second copy in another tab. Read the error, find the process that causes it, and start the second server on a free port instead without stopping the first.

hints: The message mentions `Address already in use`.
`lsof -nP -i :8000` identifies the owner. Pick a port nobody uses, such as 8001.

why.text: A port can be bound by one process at a time for a given address. The error is the kernel refusing the second `bind()`. `lsof` shows who holds it, and the fix is either to stop the owner or to choose another port.

blocks.title: Map your own LAN

task.text: On your home network, run a discovery scan of your own subnet (`{{subnet}}`), list the IPs that answered, and then scan only the 100 most common ports on one device you own, saving the normal output to `device.nmap`. Which service on that device did you not expect?

hints: `sudo nmap -sn -n SUBNET` gives discovery. Use `--top-ports 100 --open` for the port scan.

why.text: Discovery first limits the port scan to hosts that exist. `--top-ports 100` is quick and polite. The unexpected service is the audit finding: decide whether to turn it off, restrict it, or document it.

blocks.title: Read the states

task.text: Below is the state count from a server that has been running for two days. One number looks like a bug in a program, one is normal. Which is which, and what would you do next?

hints: Which side of the connection is waiting for which?
blocks.solution:
CLOSE_WAIT is the bug: the remote side closed 652 connections and the local program never closed its end. TIME_WAIT is normal after many short connections.
Find the owner with: lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:CLOSE_WAIT | awk 'NR > 1 {print $1, $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

why.text: `CLOSE_WAIT` means the kernel has acknowledged the peer's FIN and is waiting for the local application to call `close()`. A growing pile means a leak that will eventually exhaust file descriptors. `TIME_WAIT` is the kernel's housekeeping after a close and clears itself.

questions.q: A connection to a port fails instantly with "Connection refused". What does that tell you?

options.text: The host is reachable but nothing is listening on that port

questions.why: A reset comes back from a live host immediately. A silent firewall or a missing host produces a timeout instead.

questions.q: What does a growing number of `CLOSE_WAIT` sockets on your server usually mean?

options.text: The local program is not closing sockets after the peer closed them

questions.why: In CLOSE_WAIT the peer has finished and the kernel waits for the local application to call close(). A pile points to a leak in that program.

questions.q: Which command shows which process listens on TCP port 3000 on your Mac?
questions.why: macOS `netstat` has no process option and there is no `ss`. `lsof -i` maps sockets to processes.

questions.q: In the line `tcp4  0  0  192.168.1.23.52814  140.82.121.3.443  ESTABLISHED`, which number is the server's port?
questions.why: The address and port are separated by the last dot. The foreign (remote) side is `140.82.121.3.443`, so the server port is 443; `52814` is your Mac's ephemeral port.

questions.q: Which nmap option skips host discovery and scans every address as if it were up?
questions.why: `-Pn` treats all hosts as online. `-sn` is the opposite: discovery only, no port scan.

options.text: any address as long as you use -T2
your neighbor's router, if their Wi-Fi is open
your own machines and networks, and scanme.nmap.org lightly
your employer's network, if you are on the guest Wi-Fi

questions.why: Authorization is the rule, not the scan speed. Own machines and explicitly permitted targets only.

blocks.title: lan-inventory, your network as a CSV

blocks.text: Build `lan-inventory.zsh`: it sweeps your own /24, finds the live hosts from the ARP table, scans their most common ports with nmap, and writes `ip,mac,port,service` rows to a CSV. It uses everything from the last chapters: `ipconfig`, `ping`, `arp`, `xargs`, `awk`, `nmap` and `comm`.
Run this only on a network you administer. The script asks for confirmation and prints the range it will scan.
Step 1: Wake the ARP table

A ping sweep sends one probe to every address in the /24. Even a device that ignores ping answers ARP, so the kernel's ARP table fills in. Try the sweep by hand (it takes a few seconds), then read the table:

blocks.code:
seq 1 254 | xargs -P 64 -I{} ping -c 1 -t 1 -q 192.168.1.{} > /dev/null 2>&1
arp -an

blocks.text: Step 2: Extract live hosts

`arp -an` lines look like `? (192.168.1.50) at dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8 on en0 ifscope [ethernet]`. Unanswered entries say `(incomplete)`, and broadcast and multicast entries must go. Filter with awk and keep the IP and MAC as tab-separated fields:
Step 3: The script
It also adds your own address, because the ARP table never lists the machine you are on.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# lan-inventory.zsh: list live hosts on YOUR OWN /24 and their open TCP ports.
# Usage: ./lan-inventory.zsh [prefix]      e.g. ./lan-inventory.zsh 192.168.1
setopt pipefail

iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
myip=$(ipconfig getifaddr "$iface" 2>/dev/null)
prefix=${1:-${myip%.*}}
[[ -n $prefix ]] || { print -u2 "cannot find a LAN address; pass a prefix like 192.168.1"; exit 1; }

read -q "?Scan ${prefix}.0/24? Only do this on a network you own [y/N] " || { print; exit 1; }
print

out=inventory-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).csv
arpmap=$(mktemp)
hosts=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f $arpmap $hosts' EXIT

print -u2 "1/3 sweeping ${prefix}.0/24 ..."
seq 1 254 | xargs -P 64 -I{} ping -c 1 -t 1 -q "${prefix}.{}" > /dev/null 2>&1

print -u2 "2/3 reading the ARP table ..."
arp -an | awk -v p="(${prefix}." \
  'index($2, p) == 1 && $4 != "(incomplete)" && $2 !~ /\.255\)/ {gsub(/[()]/, "", $2); print $2 "\t" $4}' \
  | sort -t. -k4 -n > $arpmap
[[ -n $myip && $myip == ${prefix}.* ]] && print "${myip}\tself" >> $arpmap
cut -f1 $arpmap | sort -t. -k4 -n -u > $hosts
print -u2 "    $(wc -l < $hosts | tr -d ' ') hosts found"

print -u2 "3/3 scanning the top 100 TCP ports ..."
print "ip,mac,port,service" > $out
nmap -sT -n --open --top-ports 100 -iL $hosts -oG - 2> /dev/null \
  | awk -F'\t' '
      FNR == NR { mac[$1] = $2; next }
      /Ports:/ {
        split($1, h, " "); ip = h[2]
        sub(/^Ports: /, "", $2); n = split($2, p, ", ")
        for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
          split(p[i], f, "/")
          if (f[2] == "open") print ip "," mac[ip] "," f[1] "," f[5]
        }
      }' $arpmap - >> $out

print "wrote $out"
column -s, -t < $out
chmod +x lan-inventory.zsh && ./lan-inventory.zsh

$ ./lan-inventory.zsh
Scan 192.168.1.0/24? Only do this on a network you own [y/N] y
1/3 sweeping 192.168.1.0/24 ...
2/3 reading the ARP table ...
    6 hosts found
3/3 scanning the top 100 TCP ports ...
wrote inventory-20261008-0941.csv
ip            mac                port  service
192.168.1.1   a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9   53    domain
192.168.1.1   a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9   80    http
192.168.1.1   a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9   443   https
192.168.1.50  dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8  22    ssh
192.168.1.50  dc:a6:32:7e:41:b8  80    http
192.168.1.60  0:11:32:aa:3:5d    445   microsoft-ds

blocks.text: macOS prints MAC addresses without leading zeros (`a4:2b:b0:5c:11:9`). They are still unique, but pad them if another tool needs the standard form.
Step 4: Use the CSV
Everything from earlier chapters now applies to your own data:

blocks.code:
cut -d, -f1 inventory-*.csv | tail -n +2 | sort -u | wc -l
awk -F, 'NR > 1 {print $4}' inventory-*.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
awk -F, '$3 == 22 {print $1}' inventory-*.csv

blocks.text: Run it monthly and `diff` or `comm -13` the CSVs to catch new devices and new open ports. Add hostnames with `dscacheutil -q host -a ip_address` or `dig -x`. Rewrite the awk join in Python with `csv` once you reach the Python chapters, and use `socket.connect_ex` in a thread pool to replace nmap: you will build exactly that in [Python for networking](#py-net).
Try it in the practice terminal

The simulator has a canned LAN (`192.168.1.0/24`) and the saved `scan.txt`. Its `nmap`, `nc`, `lsof` and `netstat` give fixed output, so you can rehearse the pipelines from this chapter safely, then run them on your real network.
Glossary and next steps
Next: [Packet capture](#capture) shows the same traffic from the inside: you will watch the SYN, SYN+ACK and ACK of a real connection, and the DNS lookup before it, in tcpdump and Wireshark.

terms.def: An endpoint for network communication; the kernel gives a program a file descriptor for it
A 16-bit number that routes arriving data to the right socket on a host
Protocol, local IP, local port, remote IP and remote port: the identity of a connection
A temporary client-side port the kernel picks, 49152 to 65535 on macOS
The local address a server listens on: 127.0.0.1 (this machine only) or 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces)
The TCP state of a server socket waiting for connections
The state in which the kernel keeps a closed connection a short while to absorb stray packets
The state when the peer has closed but the local program has not; many of them indicate a leak
The first text a service sends when you connect, often its name and version
Probing many ports on a host to see which answer; legal only with authorization
The nmap phase that decides which addresses are alive
An nmap port state meaning probes get no answer, usually because a firewall drops them
Nmap Scripting Engine: scripts that extend nmap with checks such as http-title and ssl-cert
nc, a tool that connects a TCP or UDP socket to stdin and stdout
